question: Why do you want to study aerospace engineering specifically, rather than mechanical or general engineering?
lookingFor: A specific pull toward flight or space, not a generic love of engineering, backed by something concrete you did about it.

bullets: Name the specific moment or experience that pulled you toward aircraft or spacecraft, not engineering in general
Explain what aerospace has that a broader mechanical degree doesn't for your goals
Back it with something you actually did, not just admiration
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I built model gliders as a kid and got obsessed with why some designs flew straight and others spiralled into the ground, which turned into reading about airfoil shapes on my own. Mechanical engineering interested me too, but aerospace is the one field where every decision is shaped by weight and drag in a way nothing else is, and that constraint is what I find genuinely exciting to work within. Last year I built and flew a small drone and spent more time tuning the flight controller than I did assembling it, which told me this is the specific problem I want to spend years on.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I love planes' with no deeper reason
Describing generic engineering interest that doesn't explain the aerospace choice
No personal evidence, just stated enthusiasm
followUps: What's the difference between what an aerospace engineer and a mechanical engineer actually work on day to day?

question: Why do you want to study aerospace engineering at this university in particular?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to this course's structure, labs, or people, not prestige alone.

bullets: Name a specific lab, wind tunnel, project, or module that fits your interests
Connect it to something concrete you've done or want to do
Show you compared it against alternatives and chose deliberately
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Your course has a dedicated propulsion module with hands-on access to a small wind tunnel in second year, which most courses I looked at only offer as an elective in the final year. That matters to me because I want to test things with my hands, not just simulate them, and my experience building and testing a small rocket motor at school taught me how much I learn from that gap between theory and what actually happens. I also looked at two other courses with similar rankings, but this one lets me specialise toward propulsion earlier, which is the direction I already know I want to go.

commonMistakes: Citing only league table position or general reputation
Vague praise that would apply to any aerospace course
No evidence of comparing this course against others
followUps: What would you want to get out of that lab access specifically?

question: What first got you interested in flight or space?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific origin story that shows sustained rather than sudden interest.

bullets: Give a specific, real moment rather than a vague 'always loved space'
Show the interest has been sustained, not a one-off spark
Link it to what you've since done to pursue it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My uncle works in air traffic control, and he took me up in a small light aircraft when I was eleven, which is the first time I actually understood that flying is just physics being managed in real time by a person. I started reading about how wings generate lift not long after, and it never really let go of me. By the time I was choosing my A-levels I'd already spent two summers volunteering at a local gliding club, so this wasn't a sudden decision, it's been building for years.

commonMistakes: A generic 'I've always loved space' with no specific memory
An interest that sounds recently manufactured for the interview
No connection between the origin story and later actions
followUps: How has that early interest changed or matured since then?

question: Tell us about a project or hands-on experience you've had that's relevant to aerospace, like model rocketry, drone building, or gliding.
lookingFor: A concrete project with genuine technical detail and evidence of what you learned from it going wrong or working.

bullets: Describe the project specifically enough to prove you actually did it
Include a real technical detail or problem you had to solve
Reflect on what it taught you and how it shaped your interest
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I built a fixed-wing drone from a kit but modified the wing to have a higher aspect ratio because I wanted to see the effect on glide efficiency, and it made the aircraft much harder to control in crosswinds, which I hadn't predicted. I had to add a bigger vertical stabiliser to fix the yaw instability, and only then understood viscerally why real aircraft design is such a balancing act between competing goals rather than optimising one thing. It's the project that convinced me I wanted to study the underlying aerodynamics properly instead of just tinkering.

commonMistakes: Describing a project too vaguely to sound credible
Listing what was built with no problem or learning
Overclaiming solo credit for a heavily guided kit project
followUps: What would you change if you built it again?

question: What have you read or watched recently about aerospace that stuck with you?
lookingFor: Genuine intellectual engagement beyond the syllabus, with specific content and your own take on it.

bullets: Name something specific, a book, article, talk, or documentary
Summarise the actual content briefly and accurately
Give your own reaction or opinion, not just a summary
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read Stuff Matters by Mark Miodownik, and the chapter on how carbon fibre composites changed aircraft design stuck with me because it explained the trade-off so clearly, you save huge amounts of weight but you lose the way metal gives you a visible warning before it fails. That made me start reading about how engineers test composite structures for fatigue instead, since you can't just look for a dent the way you might with aluminium. It changed how I think about material choice, it's never just about strength, it's about how a material fails and whether you can see it coming.

commonMistakes: Naming a source with no real detail about its content
Reciting facts with no personal opinion or reaction
Choosing something too generic, like 'watching SpaceX launches'
followUps: Did it change your opinion on anything, or just add information?

question: Can you explain the four forces that act on an aircraft in flight?
lookingFor: A clear, correct explanation of lift, weight, thrust, and drag, and how they relate to each other in steady flight.

bullets: Name all four forces correctly: lift, weight, thrust, drag
Explain the opposing pairs, lift versus weight, thrust versus drag
State that steady level flight means the pairs are balanced
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There's lift, which acts upward and is generated mainly by the wings, and weight, which acts downward due to gravity. Then there's thrust, which pushes the aircraft forward from the engines, and drag, which resists that forward motion. In steady, level, unaccelerated flight, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag, so the aircraft isn't speeding up, slowing down, climbing, or descending. If you increase thrust beyond what balances drag, the extra energy typically goes into climbing or accelerating, which is why pilots manage all four together rather than one at a time.

commonMistakes: Naming only two or three of the four forces
Confusing which forces oppose which
Not connecting the forces to what steady flight actually means
followUps: What happens to these forces during a climb?

question: In your own words, how does a wing actually generate lift?
lookingFor: An honest, physically grounded explanation that goes beyond the oversimplified 'equal transit time' myth.

bullets: Explain that the wing deflects air downward, and by Newton's third law the air pushes back up on the wing
Mention the pressure difference between the upper and lower surface as the aerodynamic description of the same effect
Avoid presenting the flawed equal-transit-time explanation as complete
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The way I understand it, the wing's shape and angle of attack cause the air flowing over it to be deflected downward as it leaves the trailing edge, and by Newton's third law that downward push on the air produces an equal and opposite upward reaction on the wing. Looking at it from a pressure perspective, that same deflection creates lower pressure above the wing and higher pressure below, and the pressure difference integrated over the surface is what we measure as lift. I used to think it was purely about the air over the top having to travel further and arrive at the same time, but that explanation doesn't actually hold up, since it doesn't require equal transit time at all.

commonMistakes: Stating the equal transit time myth as the full explanation
Only mentioning pressure difference with no physical cause behind it
Confusing lift with thrust
followUps: Why does increasing the angle of attack increase lift, up to a point?

question: What is a stall, and why does it happen?
lookingFor: A correct understanding that stall is about angle of attack and flow separation, not about speed or engine failure.

bullets: Define stall as a loss of lift due to flow separation, not engine failure
Link stall to exceeding a critical angle of attack rather than to low speed alone
Note that stall can happen at any speed if the angle of attack is high enough
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A stall happens when the angle of attack gets too high and the airflow over the wing separates from the surface instead of following it smoothly, so the wing suddenly loses most of its lift. People often think it's about flying too slowly, and low speed is a common cause because pilots need a higher angle of attack to generate enough lift at low speed, but the real trigger is the angle of attack itself, not the speed directly. That's why an aircraft can stall at high speed too, if it pulls too hard into a steep manoeuvre and exceeds the critical angle.

commonMistakes: Defining stall as the engine cutting out
Saying stall is purely a function of speed with no mention of angle of attack
Implying stall can't happen at high speed
followUps: How do pilots recover from a stall?

question: How does a rocket generate thrust, given that there's no air to push against in space?
lookingFor: Correct application of Newton's third law, showing the applicant understands rockets don't need to push against air.

bullets: Explain thrust as the reaction to expelling mass, not pushing against surrounding air
State Newton's third law explicitly
Confirm this is why rockets work in a vacuum unlike jet engines that need atmospheric oxygen
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A rocket carries its own propellant, and it burns that fuel and expels the hot exhaust gas out the back at very high speed. By Newton's third law, for every action there's an equal and opposite reaction, so pushing that mass backward pushes the rocket forward, and this works whether or not there's air outside, because the rocket isn't pushing against the atmosphere at all. That's actually why rockets work better in a vacuum than jets do, jet engines need atmospheric oxygen to burn their fuel, while rockets carry their own oxidiser, which is also why they're so much heavier for the same thrust.

commonMistakes: Claiming the rocket pushes against the air behind it
Not naming Newton's third law explicitly when asked directly
Confusing rocket and jet engine oxygen requirements
followUps: Why do rockets need to carry an oxidiser but jet engines don't?

question: What's the fundamental difference between how a jet engine and a rocket engine work?
lookingFor: A clear technical distinction based on oxidiser source and operating environment, not just 'one is for planes, one is for space'.

bullets: State that jet engines draw in and compress atmospheric air, using its oxygen to burn fuel
State that rockets carry both fuel and oxidiser onboard, so they don't depend on the atmosphere
Connect this to why jets are more efficient in atmosphere and rockets are necessary beyond it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A jet engine takes in surrounding air, compresses it, mixes it with fuel, burns that mixture, and expels the exhaust to produce thrust, so it depends entirely on the atmosphere for its oxygen. A rocket engine carries both its fuel and its own oxidiser onboard, so it burns and expels exhaust regardless of whether there's air outside at all, which is what lets it operate in space. The trade-off is that jets are far more efficient within the atmosphere because they don't have to carry heavy oxidiser, while rockets are the only option once you leave it, which is why launch vehicles use rockets but nearly all aircraft use jets or propellers.

commonMistakes: Only distinguishing them by use case, planes versus space, without the mechanism
Forgetting that jets rely on atmospheric oxygen
Confusing thrust generation with lift generation
followUps: Why would you never see a commercial airliner powered by a rocket engine?

question: What changes about airflow when an aircraft goes from subsonic to supersonic speed?
lookingFor: Awareness that compressibility effects and shock waves fundamentally change the physics, not just 'it goes faster'.

bullets: Mention that air can no longer be treated as incompressible once speeds approach the speed of sound
Reference shock wave formation and the sudden pressure and density changes across them
Note practical consequences like the sonic boom or the need for different wing and nose designs
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Below the speed of sound, air behaves almost like an incompressible fluid for most calculations, it moves smoothly out of the way of the aircraft. As you approach and pass the speed of sound, that assumption breaks down completely, air starts to compress and shock waves form, which are very thin regions where pressure, density, and temperature jump almost instantaneously. That's why supersonic aircraft need different design choices, like thinner wings and sharper leading edges, and why the transition produces the sonic boom, which is essentially the shock wave reaching the ground. I'll admit this is an area I've only read about at an introductory level, not something I've worked through mathematically yet.

commonMistakes: Saying supersonic flight is just subsonic flight but faster
Never mentioning shock waves or compressibility at all
Bluffing confidence on a topic clearly beyond pre-university level instead of being honest about the limit of their knowledge
followUps: Why do supersonic aircraft often have thinner, sharper wings than subsonic ones?

question: Why do modern aircraft use composite materials like carbon fibre alongside or instead of aluminium?
lookingFor: Understanding of the strength-to-weight trade-off and awareness that the switch isn't without downsides.

bullets: Explain the strength-to-weight advantage of composites over traditional aluminium alloys
Mention that weight savings translate directly into fuel efficiency and range
Acknowledge a genuine trade-off, such as cost, repair difficulty, or how composites fail differently than metal
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Carbon fibre composites offer a much better strength-to-weight ratio than aluminium, so you can build a structure that's just as strong but significantly lighter, and since fuel burn scales heavily with weight, that translates directly into better fuel efficiency and longer range, which is a big part of why aircraft like the Boeing 787 use so much more composite material than older designs. The trade-off is that composites are more expensive to manufacture and much harder to inspect for damage, because they can fail internally through delamination without any visible dent on the surface the way metal would show. So it's not a straightforward upgrade, it's a genuine engineering trade-off between weight savings and inspection and repair complexity.

commonMistakes: Saying composites are simply 'better' with no trade-off mentioned
Not connecting weight reduction to fuel efficiency or performance
Vague answer with no specific material comparison
followUps: How would you inspect a composite wing for hidden damage?

question: Why do aircraft structures need to be tested for fatigue, not just maximum load?
lookingFor: Understanding that repeated cyclic loading below the ultimate strength can still cause failure over time.

bullets: Define fatigue as failure from repeated cyclic loading well below the material's ultimate strength
Explain that an aircraft experiences thousands of load cycles over its life, from pressurisation, turbulence, and landings
Reference the practical consequence, scheduled inspections or component replacement based on fatigue life, not just static strength
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A structure can handle a single load far above what it experiences in normal flight and still fail after enough repeated cycles at much lower stress, because microscopic cracks form and slowly grow with every cycle until the part suddenly fractures. An aircraft fuselage gets pressurised and depressurised on every single flight, and wings flex constantly through turbulence and manoeuvring, so over tens of thousands of flights that's an enormous number of stress cycles. That's why engineers calculate fatigue life and schedule inspections or replacements around it, rather than just checking that the structure survives one worst-case load, because a part can pass every static test and still fail from fatigue years later. I first read about this properly after looking into why the de Havilland Comet had those early fuselage failures.

commonMistakes: Confusing fatigue failure with simple overload failure
Not mentioning that fatigue happens well below ultimate strength
Treating a single load test as sufficient for certifying a structure
followUps: What real-world incident do you know of that was caused by fatigue failure?

question: Why doesn't a satellite in orbit just fall back to Earth?
lookingFor: Correct understanding that orbit is continuous falling with enough sideways velocity to keep missing the ground, not an absence of gravity.

bullets: Reject the common misconception that there's no gravity in orbit
Explain orbit as falling with enough tangential velocity that the curve of the fall matches the curve of the Earth
Mention that this is a balance, not an absence, of gravitational force
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Gravity is still very much acting on a satellite in orbit, that's actually the whole point, it's what keeps the satellite curving back toward Earth instead of flying off in a straight line. A satellite is essentially falling continuously, but it's also moving sideways so fast that by the time it falls, the curvature of its path matches the curvature of the Earth, so it keeps missing the ground. It's not that gravity is absent up there, it's that the satellite has exactly the right horizontal speed for its altitude to keep falling around the planet instead of into it.

commonMistakes: Claiming there's no gravity in orbit
Describing orbit as something other than continuous free fall
Confusing orbital velocity with escape velocity
followUps: What would happen if the satellite's speed dropped too low for its altitude?

question: What do you understand about the growing problem of space debris, and why does it matter for future missions?
lookingFor: Awareness of a real current issue in the field with some understanding of scale and consequence, not just a headline.

bullets: Explain what space debris is, defunct satellites, spent stages, and collision fragments
Reference the risk it poses, including the Kessler syndrome scenario of cascading collisions
Show awareness of what's being done or debated, tracking, deorbiting, or design-for-demise rules
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Space debris is basically the accumulation of dead satellites, spent rocket stages, and fragments from past collisions or explosions, all travelling at orbital speeds where even a small piece can seriously damage or destroy a working spacecraft. What worries me about it is the Kessler syndrome idea, that a collision creates more debris, which raises the odds of further collisions, and in the worst case certain orbits could become too dangerous to use at all. I've read that agencies are starting to require newer satellites to have deorbit plans and that companies are working on active debris removal missions, but it still feels like the regulation is lagging behind how fast we're launching things, especially with mega-constellations.

commonMistakes: Vague awareness with no specific mechanism or terminology
Not mentioning any consequence or risk, just stating debris exists
Overstating certainty about a complex, evolving policy area
followUps: What would you do differently if you were designing a satellite's end-of-life plan?

question: What's your view on the shift toward reusable rockets, and what engineering challenges do you think it introduces?
lookingFor: A genuine opinion grounded in real engineering trade-offs, not just enthusiasm for a company or launch footage.

bullets: State a clear position with reasoning, not just excitement
Identify a real engineering challenge reusability introduces, such as thermal stress, inspection burden, or added mass for landing systems
Show awareness that reusability is a trade-off against payload capacity or complexity, not a pure win
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think reusability is genuinely one of the most important shifts in the industry, because the cost per launch has come down so much that it's changed what missions are even economically possible. But it's not a free win, every stage that comes back through the atmosphere and lands has to survive intense thermal and structural stress repeatedly, so the inspection and refurbishment process between flights becomes a serious engineering problem in its own right, not just the landing itself. There's also a real payload penalty, carrying landing legs, extra fuel margin, and grid fins all add mass that a fully expendable rocket wouldn't need, so it's a genuine trade-off between per-launch cost and per-launch capability, not simply better in every way.

commonMistakes: Pure fan enthusiasm with no engineering substance
Ignoring the payload or complexity trade-offs entirely
Treating one company's approach as the only way reusability could work
followUps: Do you think reusability makes sense for every type of launch vehicle, or only some?

question: Aerospace covers both aircraft and spacecraft. Do you know which direction, aeronautical or astronautical, you're more drawn to, and why?
lookingFor: Genuine reflection on the breadth of the field with an honest, reasoned leaning rather than a forced firm answer.

bullets: Show understanding that aeronautics and astronautics are related but genuinely different sub-fields
Give an honest current leaning with a reason, or explain why it's genuinely too early to say
Demonstrate openness to the degree changing that view
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I lean more toward aeronautics, specifically propulsion, because the projects I've enjoyed most have all been about efficiency within the atmosphere, things like engine cycles and fuel burn. Astronautics interests me too, especially orbital mechanics, but I know a lot less about it in real depth, so I'd rather be honest that my current leaning is based on what I've actually had hands-on exposure to rather than a fully informed choice. Part of why I want a broad first year is precisely to test that assumption before committing to a specialisation.

commonMistakes: Claiming total certainty about a specialisation with no reasoning
Not knowing the two sub-fields are meaningfully different at all
Sounding indifferent, as if the distinction doesn't matter to them
followUps: What would change your mind between the two?

question: What is a wind tunnel used for, and why can't engineers rely purely on computer simulations instead?
lookingFor: Understanding that wind tunnels validate and complement simulation rather than being an outdated alternative to it.

bullets: Explain a wind tunnel tests a model or component under controlled, measurable airflow conditions
State that simulations rely on models and assumptions that need real-world validation
Note that both are used together in modern practice, not one replacing the other
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A wind tunnel lets engineers put a scale model, or sometimes a full-size component, into a controlled airstream and directly measure things like lift, drag, and pressure distribution, rather than only predicting them. The reason simulations alone aren't enough is that computational fluid dynamics still relies on simplified turbulence models and assumptions, so its results need to be checked against real physical data to know how accurate they actually are for a given design. In practice modern aerospace design uses both together, simulation to explore many design variants quickly and cheaply, and wind tunnel testing to validate and refine the most promising ones before committing to a full build.

commonMistakes: Treating wind tunnels as outdated technology replaced entirely by simulation
Describing a wind tunnel with no mention of what it actually measures
Not explaining why simulation alone has limits
followUps: What's one thing a wind tunnel can tell you that a simulation might get wrong?

question: Why does the position of an aircraft's centre of gravity matter for its stability?
lookingFor: Understanding of the relationship between centre of gravity, centre of lift, and pitch stability.

bullets: Explain that stability depends on the relative position of the centre of gravity to the centre of lift
Describe what happens if the centre of gravity is too far aft, reduced or negative stability
Mention practical consequences, like weight and balance limits on real aircraft
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The aircraft's centre of gravity needs to sit in a specific range relative to the centre of lift for the aircraft to be naturally stable in pitch, meaning if it's disturbed it tends to return to level flight rather than diverging further away from it. If the centre of gravity moves too far aft, toward or behind the centre of lift, the aircraft becomes less stable and can even become dangerously unpredictable to control, which is why airlines have strict weight and balance calculations for every flight based on passenger and cargo loading. It's a good example of how a purely structural or loading decision, where the cargo sits, directly becomes a flight safety issue.

commonMistakes: Not connecting centre of gravity to the centre of lift at all
Describing centre of gravity as only a structural, not a flight-dynamics, concern
Vague statement that balance 'matters' with no mechanism given
followUps: Why do airlines calculate weight and balance separately for every single flight?

question: The Boeing 737 MAX crashes were linked to commercial pressure affecting engineering decisions. As a future engineer, how do you think about that tension between cost pressure and safety?
lookingFor: Mature ethical reasoning about a real industry event, showing understanding of engineering responsibility without naive absolutism.

bullets: Show accurate, specific awareness of what happened, not just that 'something went wrong'
Reason through the tension honestly rather than dismissing commercial pressure as simply evil
Land on a clear position about the engineer's responsibility to flag and escalate safety concerns
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: From what I understand, a big part of what went wrong was that a new flight control system, MCAS, was added to compensate for the way larger engines changed the aircraft's handling, and decisions were made to minimise how much retraining pilots would need, partly for commercial reasons, which meant some safety-critical information wasn't surfaced clearly enough to pilots or regulators. I don't think commercial pressure itself is the villain, cost and schedule matter in any real engineering job, and pretending otherwise is naive, but I do think engineers have a specific responsibility to make risk visible even when it's inconvenient, and to insist that safety-critical assumptions get properly tested and documented rather than quietly accepted. If I were in that position, I'd want the process to protect an engineer who raises a serious safety concern, rather than one where raising it is career risk in itself, because that's ultimately what determines whether concerns get surfaced in time.

commonMistakes: Vague or inaccurate description of what actually happened
Treating commercial pressure as automatically illegitimate with no nuance
No clear personal position on engineering responsibility
followUps: What would you do if you personally spotted a safety concern that management wanted to downplay?

question: What development in aerospace over the next twenty years excites or interests you the most, and why?
lookingFor: A specific, informed area of genuine interest with reasoning, showing the applicant follows the field beyond headlines.

bullets: Name a specific, real development, not a vague 'space travel will improve'
Explain the actual technical challenge involved, showing some depth
Give a genuine personal reason for the interest, not just that it sounds impressive
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I find electric and hybrid-electric propulsion for short-haul aircraft genuinely exciting, because battery energy density is still nowhere near jet fuel, so the engineering challenge isn't just building an electric motor, it's rethinking the entire aircraft around a completely different weight and range trade-off. What draws me to it specifically is that it's not a solved problem being scaled up, it's still genuinely open, companies are trying very different architectures and nobody's proven the winning approach yet. I like that it sits at the intersection of propulsion and structures, since a lighter airframe changes what battery range becomes viable, which is exactly the kind of whole-system thinking I want to get good at.

commonMistakes: Vague excitement about 'the future of space' with no specific technology named
No mention of the actual technical challenge involved
Reciting a headline with no personal reasoning behind the interest
followUps: What's the biggest technical obstacle standing in the way of that becoming widespread?

question: Which parts of your maths and physics studies so far do you think will be most useful in aerospace engineering, and why?
lookingFor: Genuine connection between specific coursework and real aerospace applications, showing preparedness.

bullets: Name specific maths or physics topics, not just 'maths in general'
Explain the concrete link to an aerospace application
Show honest awareness of where the gap between school level and degree level will be
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Mechanics has probably been the most directly useful so far, especially forces, moments, and circular motion, because those show up immediately when you start thinking about lift, orbits, and stability. Calculus matters too, particularly differential equations, since I've read that a lot of flight dynamics and control theory comes down to solving them, even though I've only worked with fairly simple ones at school level so far. I know the degree will take that much further into things like vector calculus and numerical methods that I haven't touched yet, so I see my current maths as a genuine foundation rather than something that's already sufficient.

commonMistakes: Vague claim that 'all maths and physics helps' with no specifics
Overstating current maths level as already sufficient for the degree
No link drawn between the school topic and an aerospace application
followUps: What area of maths do you feel least confident in right now?

question: What historical or recent aerospace achievement do you find most impressive, and why?
lookingFor: A specific, well-understood example with reasoning about why it's technically impressive, not just famous.

bullets: Name a specific event or project, with accurate basic facts
Explain what made it technically difficult or novel at the time
Give a personal reason it resonates, not just that it's well known
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I find the Apollo Guidance Computer landing the lunar module genuinely astonishing, because it did that with a fraction of the processing power of a modern calculator, using software the astronauts could interrupt and re-prioritise mid-descent when alarms started going off. What impresses me isn't just the raw achievement, it's that the team built enough margin and clear failure-handling into the system that a computer overload alarm didn't abort the whole mission, it just meant the system dropped lower-priority tasks and kept doing the landing calculation. It's the example I come back to when people assume more advanced engineering always just means more powerful hardware, sometimes it means better judgment about what actually matters under pressure.

commonMistakes: Naming something famous with no specific technical detail
Factually incorrect details about the chosen example
No personal reasoning, just restating why it's generally considered significant
followUps: Is there a more recent example that impresses you in the same way?

question: What kind of aerospace problem do you eventually want to work on, and how does this course get you there?
lookingFor: A believable, specific direction connected honestly to the course content, with room to still be exploring.

bullets: Give a specific area of interest, not a vague 'work in the industry'
Connect it to a real feature of the course, module, or research group
Stay honest about flexibility, this is a direction not a locked-in plan
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd like to end up working on more efficient jet engine design, since that's where I think aerospace can make the biggest near-term difference to emissions without needing an entirely new kind of aircraft. Your course's propulsion stream in the final two years, plus the option to do a project with the turbomachinery research group, is exactly the pathway that gets me from where I am now to being useful in that field. I know that plan could easily shift once I've actually studied thermodynamics and fluid mechanics properly, and I'm fine with that, the point right now is that I have a real direction pulling me rather than just a general interest in the industry.

commonMistakes: A goal too vague to connect meaningfully to the course
Overly rigid five-year plan with no acknowledgment it might change
No specific link to what the course actually offers
followUps: What's the first step you'd want to take toward that after graduating?

subtopic: Handling difficult teamwork on a technical project
question: Aerospace projects are built by large teams. Tell us about a time you had to work with others on a technical project, and how you handled disagreement over a design decision.
lookingFor: A STAR-structured example showing collaborative, evidence-based problem solving on something technical.

bullets: Set up a specific technical project with a real disagreement, not a vague team story
Show the resolution was based on evidence or testing, not just compromise for its own sake
Reflect on what it taught about working in engineering teams specifically
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: For a school engineering project we built a small trebuchet-style launcher, and I wanted to add a counterweight release mechanism while a teammate thought it added unnecessary complexity and risk of failure on the day. Instead of just arguing about it, we agreed to build a quick prototype of both versions and test them against each other, which showed the release mechanism did add meaningful range but also introduced a jam risk we hadn't considered. We ended up using a simplified version of my idea with a safety pin my teammate suggested, which fixed the jam issue, and the final version outperformed either of our original proposals. It taught me that in engineering, disagreements are usually best settled by building and testing something small rather than debating in the abstract.

commonMistakes: A vague teamwork story with no real technical disagreement
Framing the story as themselves being simply right and the teammate wrong
No connection to the fact that aerospace work is inherently large-team and technical
followUps: What would you have done if the test results had been inconclusive?
